# OxyLux Solutions — full reference

## Treatment
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy means breathing concentrated oxygen inside a chamber pressurized above normal air pressure. The added pressure lets oxygen dissolve into blood plasma so more of it can reach tissue that is healing. A session typically lasts 60 to 90 minutes; plan on about two hours for the first visit.

OxyLux uses an Oxycell OxyPro Genesis hard-shell chamber with a padded reclining seat, a wide window, soft lighting and an intercom to the attendant, who controls pressure and oxygen from a touchscreen outside the chamber. One patient per chamber. Surfaces are disinfected between patients.

HBOT is FDA-cleared for specific conditions, including diabetic and other non-healing wounds and tissue damage after radiation therapy. Other uses are considered off-label. Patients also use HBOT to support recovery before and after surgery or cosmetic procedures, and for sports recovery. No outcome is guaranteed.

## Who should wait or talk to a doctor first
High fever, ear infection or blocked ear canal, sinus or upper respiratory infection, air travel in the last 24 hours, untreated or recent pneumothorax (collapsed lung), severe lung or heart disease, seizure disorder, emphysema, glaucoma, optic neuritis, aneurysm, untreated asthma, certain medications (bleomycin, disulfiram, mafenide acetate) and pregnancy. Every patient completes a consent form and health screening before the first session.

## Insurance and booking
OxyLux accepts most major insurance plans. Coverage depends on the patient's plan and diagnosis; patients can call (305) 205-2738 to check before their first visit. Bring a photo ID and insurance card. Booking is online (choose a day and time, then sign the consent form) or by phone.

## What to expect
1. Reserve online and sign the consent form.
2. Arrive 15 minutes early; the team reviews health history, takes vitals and answers questions.
3. Change into the 100% cotton scrubs provided. Lotions, perfume, makeup, jewelry and electronics stay outside the chamber.
4. Pressure rises slowly; ears feel full like a plane descending. Swallowing or yawning clears them.
5. Rest, nap or listen to music while the attendant monitors the session over the intercom.
6. Pressure comes down gradually; most people return to their day right away.

## Dr. Fermin Morales, MD, FACS — Founder and Medical Director
Dr. Fermin Esteban Morales earned his medical degree in Havana, Cuba, in 1985 and has more than four decades in medicine. He completed general surgery residencies at Hospital General Docente "Dr. Carlos J. Finlay" in Havana and at Lehigh Valley Hospital in Allentown, Pennsylvania, and worked as a surgical assistant at the Miami Heart Institute. He is board certified by the American Board of Surgery and the Cuban Board of General Surgery, is a Fellow of the American College of Surgeons, and is a member of the Florida Medical Association and the Society of Laparoendoscopic Surgeons. He is a former Assistant Professor of Surgery at Penn State University and Florida International University, practices general and cosmetic surgery in Miami, and speaks English and Spanish.
